My research program asks a single question across very different historical and institutional settings: **when does regulation actually serve the public interest, and when is it better understood as protection for incumbents, a tool of bureaucratic expansion, or a substitute for order that markets and communities already provide?** A newer line of work turns the same lens on the size of government itself, asking when crisis actually enlarges the state and when competition between jurisdictions prevents it. I combine historical institutional analysis with modern econometric and panel-data methods, in the tradition of Buchanan, Tullock, and Stigler and the Austrian emphasis on knowledge problems and spontaneous order.

## Dissertation

My dissertation develops this question through three essays.

### Distillers and Chemists: Capture by Eligibility in the Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897

*Job market paper · sole-authored · Winner, 2026 SDAE Graduate Student Essay Contest*

The Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897 is conventionally remembered as one of America's first consumer-protection laws. The straight distillers of Kentucky and Pennsylvania lobbied for it against the rectifiers who compounded cheaper whiskey from neutral spirit, and the received account reads it as a raising-rivals'-costs victory. On a newly digitized state-by-fiscal-year panel built from the Commissioner of Internal Revenue's annual reports, I find the opposite of foreclosure: rectified output averaged 43 percent more after the Act than before, and the within-state gap between straight and rectified output did not shift toward straight whiskey. What the Act created was a certified segment, flat to 1902 and then fast-growing during a cultivated demand campaign, and Kentucky and Pennsylvania took 92 percent of bonded bourbon and rye withdrawals, roughly in proportion to the whiskey they already held in bond. The capture lies in the eligibility rule: in 1893 the Deputy Commissioner of Internal Revenue had proposed a cheap stamp for every bottle that would have answered the deception the distillers complained of, and the Act instead confined the stamp to whiskey four years old, writing eligibility around the aged stock the incumbents already held. Capture can be identified by whom a rule's eligibility was written around, not only by rivals' losses.

### Private Mechanisms for Stopping Diamond-Dybvig Runs: Evidence from U.S. Newspapers, 1889–1929

*with Daniel J. Smith*

Assembling a new dataset of 544 bank runs hand-coded from digitized newspapers, we document how localized runs were contained by a rich toolkit of private, market-based mechanisms, eight of them understudied. The evidence qualifies the standard case for deposit insurance and a fully developed lender of last resort.

[Summary & figures](papers/bank-runs.qmd){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm} [Companion paper (SSRN)](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5641472){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm}

### Who Killed the Green Fairy? Temperance, Language, and Wine in the Swiss Absinthe Ban of 1908

*with Nicholas A. Jensen*

Switzerland's 1908 vote to ban absinthe is usually read as a temperance triumph. Using canton-level records of both the petition and the vote, we find that organized temperance carried the petition while the wine interest appears at the ballot: holding the French-speaking share fixed, a one-point higher share of national wine revenue goes with a 0.62-point higher yes-share. The same specification finds no wine effect on six unrelated federal ballots.

[Download Paper (PDF)](https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/raukw6mvyrkvnse7dvd0f/jensen-absinthe.pdf?rlkey=9jku1wruib7ro02y3w04h2vw7&raw=1){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm} [Summary & figures](papers/absinthe.qmd){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm}

## Beyond the dissertation

The projects beyond the dissertation carry the same question into new terrain: whether crisis actually enlarges the state, what the repeal of a legal regime reveals about who it protected, and how the welfare state interacts with the vices it is said to subsidize.

### Uncorked: How Wall Street Priced the Repeal of Prohibition

*with Patricia Hummel and Corey Pendleton*

How did equity markets price the end of Prohibition? Dating the moments investors learned of repeal from newspaper coverage of the 1933 ratification process, we estimate abnormal returns for alcohol firms and related industries. Alcohol stocks rose when New York voted to send repeal delegates, then fell sharply in July once Alabama, Arkansas, and Tennessee made repeal certain, while most other industries barely moved. Investors priced repeal as the end of a protected market: competition would return and erode the profits the surviving firms had earned under Prohibition.

A companion paper builds a hand-verified dataset of distillery entry and enforcement events from New York newspapers, 1929–1940: 697 distinct events from 1,681 candidate hits, 677 of them enforcement actions against illicit stills and just 20 legal entries.

[Summary](papers/prohibition.qmd){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm} [Draft available on request](mailto:jrs2ge@mtmail.mtsu.edu){.btn .btn-outline-secondary .btn-sm}

### Crisis and Local Leviathan

*Work in progress · sole-authored*

This project moves from particular regulations to the size of government itself. It tests Robert Higgs's ratchet hypothesis, that emergencies permanently enlarge the state, at the level of American government where exit is cheapest. The current revision follows the annual budgets of county and city governments in metropolitan areas struck by hurricane-force winds, compared with unstruck metros in the same state, alongside the metropolitan economic freedom index.

[Project summary](papers/crisis-local-leviathan.qmd){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm}

### Alms and Ale

A further project asks whether more generous welfare states raise the demand for alcohol, using a panel of OECD countries, 1995–2023.

[Project summary](papers/alms-and-ale.qmd){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm}
